title: A New Framework for Modeling Solar Flares from MHD to Kinetic Processes

abstract_screen.rationale: It presents an MHD-to-kinetic flare modeling chain (ARMS, kglobal, RADYN+FP) covering electron and proton acceleration, transport and lower-atmosphere heating. That gives the physical context for interpreting STIX/EUI flare timing and particle acceleration, but it is a modeling paper rather than an observational or timing/QPP analysis.

problem.explanation: It addresses particle acceleration and the flare-loop response, the physics behind HXR/EUV timing. It does not study temporal variability, energy-dependent timing or QPPs; QPPs are used only to set the injection decay time.

method.explanation: Purely numerical: MHD, kinetic-hybrid and radiation-hydrodynamic simulation. No time-series, spectral-fitting or imaging-analysis techniques transfer directly to STIX/EUI data analysis.

data.explanation: No observational data are analysed. STIX and EUI are not used, and Solar Orbiter is mentioned only via SPICE in the introduction.

phenomenon.explanation: Directly concerns nonthermal electron/proton spectra, transport, return-current losses, footpoint HXR source heights, evaporation and impulsive-phase heating. These are the phenomena that STIX spectra and timing diagnose.

future.explanation: The planned 3D, multi-loop, multi-snapshot extension and parameter studies (Sec. 4) could supply synthetic HXR/EUV lightcurves to compare with STIX/EUI timing and QPP observations. The current single-injection run yields only limited directly comparable observables.

one_line: Chains the 2.5D ARMS MHD eruption model, the kglobal reconnection-acceleration model and RADYN+FP to inject self-consistent electron and proton distributions into a single newly reconnected flare loop, then follows transport, return currents, mirroring, chromospheric evaporation and condensation, white-light emission and HXR source height.
offers: Self-consistently derived electron and proton spectra from reconnection, κ≈2.9 for both, with acceleration timescale ~5τA≈24 s (Sec. 3.2, Fig. 2). A reference for the acceleration timescale and spectral hardness to compare with STIX-derived indices.

Time-dependent loop response to an exponentially decaying (τi=20 s) beam (Figs. 4–6): looptop 24–28 MK within ~1.4 s, evaporation reaching the apex at 7.3 s, apex density and temperature at 10, 20 and 40 s. Useful for sanity-checking thermal/nonthermal timing in STIX lightcurves.

Quantitative breakdown of return-current versus collisional versus mirroring losses for 20 keV electrons at 3° and 45° pitch angles (Figs. 9–11). Return-current losses of ~2.5 keV occur early and collisional losses of ~9 keV in the corona at t=5 s, which matters for interpreting low-energy spectral flattening and energy-dependent delays.

Synthetic 30–50 keV HXR emissivity height (~690 km above photosphere) co-spatial with white-light emission (Fig. 12, Sec. 3.3.2). An alternative explanation for low HXR footpoint heights invoking chromospheric compression rather than low ambient densities.
Temperature-dependent upflow/downflow crossover at 1–2 MK (Fig. 8), relevant to EUV ribbon/loop Doppler and intensity interpretation.

findings.evidence: Sec. 3.3: the injection flux decays exponentially with τi=20 s, justified by QPP intervals of 'typically about 20 s' (Hayes et al. 2020). QPPs are described as potential signatures of individual reconnection bursts (Ashfield et al. 2026). Sec. 4 lists this as an assumption and notes that only one injection episode is modelled.
findings.inference: The model treats one QPP-like burst as one injection episode, but it does not produce or test QPPs. Its value for QPP work is as a template for a single pulse's thermal and nonthermal response, not as evidence for any QPP mechanism.
findings.recommendation: Use the single-pulse response (heating rise in <1 s, evaporation filling in ~7–10 s) as a reference when deconvolving multi-pulse STIX lightcurves. Do not cite this paper as support for a QPP mechanism.

findings.evidence: Sec. 3.3 and Figs. 10–11, 9: in the first ~0.5 s the return-current electric field exceeds Dreicer at the looptop. Electrons lose ~2.5 keV to return-current losses in the corona, and high-pitch-angle electrons are reversed. Later, collisional losses dominate (9 keV at t=5 s), and after ~25 s high-pitch-angle electrons are thermalized in the corona before returning.
findings.inference: Transport effects evolve on second timescales during a single injection. Energy-dependent timing and spectral changes seen by STIX could therefore partly reflect evolving return-current and collisional conditions in the loop rather than changes at the accelerator.
findings.recommendation: When interpreting STIX spectral flattening at low energies or energy-dependent delays early in impulsive bursts, consider return-current and coronal-density evolution as alternatives to acceleration changes. Cross-reference Alaoui et al. 2021 and Allred et al. 2020.

findings.evidence: Sec. 3.3.2, Fig. 12 right: model 30–50 keV HXR emissivity peaks at the base of the compressed transition region, ~690 km above the photosphere, co-spatial with the white-light enhancement. The authors argue this matches Krucker et al. (2015) without requiring low footpoint densities.
findings.inference: This bears on interpreting HXR footpoint heights and HXR–EUV/white-light co-spatiality. It is relevant if STIX and EUI limb or near-limb events are used to locate where emission originates in ribbons.
findings.recommendation: If analysing near-limb STIX/EUI events, compare footpoint heights against this prediction and against Krucker et al. 2015.

findings.evidence: Sec. 3.2, Fig. 2: kglobal with guide field 0.3 gives κ≈2.9 for both species. The authors note this is harder than typical solar flare spectra and that the guide field strongly controls nonthermal production (Dahlin et al. 2014; Arnold et al. 2021).
findings.inference: The guide-field dependence offers a physical lever linking observed STIX spectral indices to reconnection geometry. The specific spectrum here is not representative of typical events.
findings.recommendation: Treat the kglobal spectrum as illustrative only. For linking observed spectral indices to reconnection, read Arnold et al. 2021 and Yin et al. 2024a.

findings.evidence: Sec. 3.3.1, Fig. 7: nonthermal protons experience warm-target collisions in the hot corona and deposit energy sharply at the transition region, pushing it lower. They carry ~10% of the injected energy flux in the leaky-box escape.
findings.inference: Proton heating has no direct STIX signature but could alter footpoint dynamics seen by EUI. This is mostly peripheral to an electron-focused timing study.
findings.recommendation: Note as context only; low priority.

reading.why: Statistical QPP study (typical ~20 s periods) used to set the injection timescale. Directly relevant to QPP statistics in flare X-ray lightcurves.

caveats: Pure simulation: no STIX, EUI or any observational data are analysed, so it offers no direct dataset, event or analysis technique.
Only one injection episode into one symmetric loop from a 2.5D model. No lightcurves, QPPs or multi-loop ribbon evolution are produced, so temporal-variability predictions are limited.
The 20 s injection decay time is assumed from QPP statistics, not derived. The paper does not test QPP mechanisms.
The ARMS active region is idealized (fields ~2.5 G, size ×10, rescaled by factors of 10 and 4). The kglobal spectrum (κ≈2.9) is harder than typical flare spectra.
The FP solver is time-independent per snapshot and omits runaway-electron return current, so early-time (<0.5 s) return-current losses are overestimated by the authors' own admission.
Synthetic HXR is shown only as an emissivity height profile (30–50 keV). No synthetic spectra or count lightcurves suitable for direct STIX comparison are given.
instruments_and_data: ARMS 2.5D MHD (adaptive mesh refinement) simulation of a breakout eruption
RADYN+FP radiation-hydrodynamics with multi-species Fokker–Planck transport
Synthetic 30–50 keV bremsstrahlung emissivity (Haug 1997 cross-section) and 5000 Å continuum
